name: Visa

header.one_liner: Toll road on global card volume; quality is not in question, the price already pays for it.
header.thesis: Visa converts roughly 10% payments-volume growth into low-teens EPS growth at a 59% operating margin. At 30x current earnings the market already assumes that continues; the engine's base case earns about the hurdle, so the stance is a position to challenge rather than an obvious add.

base.eps_label: FY2026E non-GAAP EPS, implied by company guidance (9M actual $9.79 plus Q4 at guided growth)
base.rev_label: FY2026E net revenue ($B): 9M actual $33.76B plus Q4 at the guided high end of low double digits

rev_cagr.why: Fiscal Q3 net revenue grew 14% (13% constant dollar) on 10% payments volume and 12% cross-border growth. Management guides Q4 to the high end of low double digits and full-year to the low end of low teens. The base case assumes three more years of a slowing low double digit rate.

margin_end.why: Non-GAAP net margin is about 54% today. The base case holds it flat because opex is guided to grow as fast as revenue (low end of low teens) and client incentives grew 18% in the quarter, faster than revenue. This is the engine's judgment, not a company number.
margin_end.source: Computed from FQ3 2026 release; opex and incentive growth as printed

share_chg.why: Visa repurchased $16.4B in nine months against a $739B market cap, about 3% annualised. Base case assumes the pace slows slightly as the price rises.

exit_pe.why: Current multiple is about 30x. The base case assumes a three-point de-rating as growth slows toward ten percent. Bear assumes regulatory or competitive pressure takes it to the low twenties. This is the most disputable number on the page.
exit_pe.source: Engine judgment; current multiple computed from price and FY26E EPS

pillars.title: Network effects convert volume into earnings
pillars.claim: Payments volume of +10% and 71.7B processed transactions (+10%) feed net revenue of +14%, because pricing and value-added services grow on top of volume.

evidence.t: Net revenue $11,633M, +14%; payments volume +10% constant dollar; processed transactions 71.7B, +10%
Data processing revenue +17% and other revenue +45%, faster than volume

pillars.test: Does net revenue growth stay above payments volume growth for the next two quarters?

pillars.title: Margin is high but not rising
pillars.claim: GAAP operating margin of 59.1% in the quarter is below the nine-month 61.7% because of $253M litigation and $563M severance. Underlying margin is stable, not expanding.

evidence.t: Total opex $4,756M, +19% in the quarter against revenue +14%
Severance of $563M recorded as personnel expense; roles cut mainly in technology and product

pillars.test: Does opex growth settle at or below revenue growth after the restructuring?

pillars.title: Client incentives are the quiet cost lever
pillars.claim: Incentives of $4,680M grew 18%, faster than revenue. They are the price Visa pays to keep issuers and processors on the network, and they are where competitive pressure would show first.
pillars.test: Do incentives as a share of gross revenue keep rising?

pillars.title: Capital return supports EPS
pillars.claim: A 2.5% to 3% annual share count reduction adds roughly three points to EPS growth.

evidence.t: Repurchases $16,430M in nine months; dividends $3,852M; quarterly dividend $0.670

pillars.test: Does the repurchase pace hold as the price sits near its 52-week high?

variant.street: The market pays about 30x current-year earnings, which prices a durable low-teens EPS compounder with little regulatory drag.
variant.ours: The engine's base case earns about the hurdle: a high-quality business at a full price. The variant view is not that Visa is weak, but that the exit multiple, not growth, decides the return.
variant.could_be_wrong: If volume growth holds at 10% and agentic commerce adds a new fee pool, a 30x multiple can persist and the bull case becomes the base case.
variant.would_change_mind: Two consecutive quarters where net revenue growth falls below 10%, or incentives growing faster than 20%.

moat.summary: Two-sided network with issuers and merchants on both sides; 59% operating margin through restructuring and litigation charges.
moat.detail: The existing Porter card (10-K based, FY2025) rates Visa Strong; the new quarter does not contradict it.

quality.leverage_note: Debt about $23.9B against cash and investments of $13.9B at 30 June 2026: modest leverage for a business earning about $28B a year pre-tax.
quality.incentive_note: Incentives to clients are rising faster than revenue; watch whether this is share defence.
checks: Tax rate 18.4% non-GAAP in the quarter
Cash conversion: nine-month operating cash flow $16.3B against GAAP net income $17.5B (timing of litigation escrow and tax)

catalysts.label: Visa fiscal Q4 2026 earnings
catalysts.note: Guide: net revenue growth high end of low double digits, EPS growth low end of mid-teens, tax rate about 19%.

tripwires.text: Net revenue growth below 10% in a quarter
Opex growth above revenue growth for two quarters
tripwires.note: Seen in one quarter so far (opex +19% vs revenue +14%); the tripwire needs two.

risks: Interchange litigation and the Credit Card Competition Act (not covered by the sources retrieved).
Account-to-account and stablecoin rails taking low-value volume.
Agentic commerce is an opportunity in the company's words, with no revenue disclosed.

lenses.eisman: Look at the incentive line, not the headline: 18% growth in what Visa pays clients is the number that would move first if the network's pricing power weakened.
lenses.munger: Invert it: what makes Visa a bad investment from here? Only the price. The business has few ways to fail.
lenses.buffett: A toll road with a 59% margin is exactly the kind of business he buys, at a price he would call full when the yield is 3.3% against a 5.2% Treasury.
lenses.hohn: A durable network with growing incentives and a restructuring: check that the cost cuts are funding reinvestment, not hiding a growth slowdown.

review.basis: Fiscal Q3 2026 10-Q (June quarter). Fiscal Q4 reports on 27 October US time; this review refreshes after the print.
review.headline: A toll road on global spending with 68% EBITDA margins. Quality is not in question; the price already assumes it lasts.
review.model: Visa runs the network that connects card-issuing banks and merchants' banks. It earns a small fee on volume and per transaction, and never lends money.

how_it_earns.v: Fees on payments volume, charged to issuers. Tracks spending.
Per-transaction fees for authorising, clearing and settling, plus value-added services.
Cross-border and currency-conversion fees. Highest margin, tracks travel and e-commerce.
Payments back to banks and merchants to win and keep volume. A contra-revenue line.

mix.note: Revenue only: Visa reports one segment. Shares are of gross revenue before client incentives, which are netted off to reach net revenue.

rows.label: International
rows.driver: Cross-border volume +14%, offset by lower FX volatility

callout.label: Value-added services
callout.text: Cuts across the lines above. Growing about a third a year and now a third of net revenue.

review.position: One of two global open-loop networks with Mastercard. Larger by revenue and market value; Mastercard is growing slightly faster.

moat.threat: Regulators and big issuers, not rivals, decide how much of the toll Visa keeps.

what_numbers_say.d: Net revenue +14% on payments volume +11% and transactions +10%. Pricing and value-added services add the gap.

what_numbers_say.t: Value-added services are the new engine
what_numbers_say.d: $3.8B in Q3, +33%. Consulting engagements up about 30%.
Client incentives +18% vs gross revenue +15%. They are now about 29% of gross revenue.
Non-GAAP opex +17% vs net revenue +14%, on marketing (World Cup) and hiring. GAAP opex +19% with $563M severance.

balance.read: Net cash-like leverage. The real liabilities are litigation and settlement guarantees, not debt.
facts: Repaid $5.6B of notes, issued $3.0B in FY2026
Interchange litigation funded by class B conversion, not class A cash

flags.flag: Litigation costs sit outside non-GAAP and outside class A
flags.evidence: $1.1B of interchange accruals in nine months, excluded from non-GAAP. They are funded by reducing class B conversion rates, so class A EPS is unaffected.
Nine-month operating cash flow $16.3B vs GAAP net income $17.5B, on litigation payments, incentive payments and tax timing.
New Brazilian rules will require Visa to extend settlement guarantees to sellers; Visa expects settlement exposure to increase.

forecast_basis.rev_cagr: Driver-based: volume plus pricing plus value-added services, fading toward 10%
forecast_basis.margin_end: Trend: held flat because opex is guided to grow with revenue
forecast_basis.share_chg: Trend: about 2.5% a year from buybacks
forecast_basis.exit_pe: Judgment: modest de-rating as growth slows

base.story: Volume grows high single digits, pricing and services add a few points, buybacks add three; EPS compounds low teens.
base.needs: No change to US interchange or routing rules

downside.story: Routing mandates or an interchange settlement cut the toll; incentives rise to defend share; the multiple falls toward the low twenties.
downside.needs: Credit Card Competition Act passes, or incentives grow above 20%

upside.story: Value-added services and agentic commerce become a second engine; growth holds at 12% and the multiple stays near 30x.
upside.needs: Services above a third of revenue with margins intact

risks.how: Routing mandates or interchange limits let merchants send transactions to cheaper networks, lowering Visa's fee per dollar.
risks.watch: Service revenue per dollar of volume

risks.cause: Big banks demand a bigger share
risks.how: Issuers are concentrated and can switch networks at renewal. Visa pays them through rising incentives.
International fees are the highest-margin line and depend on travel and currency volatility, both cyclical.
Real-time account-to-account systems (Pix, UPI) and stablecoins bypass cards, starting with small transactions in emerging markets.
Visa is investing in marketing, people and acquisitions. If that persists, the margin slips from a very high base.

peer_read.why_premium: Visa has the highest EBITDA margin in the group, the largest network, and no credit risk. Mastercard earns more on its smaller capital base.
peer_read.why_not: Mastercard grows faster on consensus and trades at a slightly lower forward EV/EBITDA, so Visa's premium over its closest twin is hard to justify on growth alone.
peer_read.peers_note: American Express is a lender, so it is compared on P/E only. PayPal trades on a very different multiple because its growth and margins are lower.

questions: Are rising incentives a cost of growth or a sign of weakening bargaining power?
Does value-added services growth carry the same margin as the core network?
Would you pay a premium to Mastercard for slower growth?
